# Line-envelope transport and an exact point-selection obstruction

This records what the exact continuous center-transversal lemma does and
does not supply. None of these statements is a mixed-integer theorem.

## 1. A valid halfspace-dominated measure on an actual line section

Let C be a convex body in R^r, r>=2, and let mu be an absolutely continuous
probability measure supported on C. Let L=c+R v, |v|=1, intersect C.
Suppose every closed halfspace containing L has mu-mass at least k>0.
Then there exists a non-atomic measure nu of total mass k, supported on
L intersect C, such that

    nu(H)<=mu(H)                                  (1)

for every closed ambient halfspace H.

Proof. For t in R write p_t=c+tv, and define

    G(t)=min_{|b|=1, b dot v>=0} mu({x:b dot (x-p_t)>=0}),
    F(t)=min_{|b|=1, b dot v<=0} mu({x:b dot (x-p_t)>=0}).

These minima exist and are continuous in t. The hemispheres of normals
are compact, and cap probabilities are jointly continuous in (t,b) by
dominated convergence, since every hyperplane is mu-null. G is
nonincreasing and F is nondecreasing.

For every t,

    F(t)+G(t)>=k.                                 (2)

To see this, choose arbitrary normals from the two hemispheres. If one
is perpendicular to v, its cap contains L and alone has mass at least k.
Otherwise take a positive linear combination of the two normals whose
component along v is zero. If the resulting vector is nonzero, its cap
through p_t contains L and is contained in the union of the two original
caps. If the resulting vector is zero, the original normals are opposite
and their two caps cover R^r. Both cases give the lower bound k on the
sum of the original cap masses. Taking the two independent minima proves
(2).

Define B(t)=max(0,k-G(t)). This is continuous and nondecreasing. Let
L intersect C={p_t:t_-<=t<=t_+}. If t<t_-, strict separation of p_t
from C supplies a zero-mass cap whose normal has negative v component:
test the separating normal on any point of L intersect C. Thus F(t)=0,
so (2) implies B(t)=0. If t>t_+, the corresponding separator has positive
v component, so G(t)=0 and B(t)=k. Hence B is the cumulative distribution
function of a non-atomic measure of mass k supported on [t_-,t_+].
Transport it to L to define nu.

For a halfspace meeting L in {p_s:s>=t}, its nu-mass is

    k-B(t)=min(k,G(t))<=G(t)<=mu(H).

For one meeting L in {p_s:s<=t}, its nu-mass is

    B(t)<=F(t)<=mu(H),

using (2). Continuity of B makes both formulas valid for the closed
halflines. A halfspace parallel to L either misses L, in which case its
nu-mass is zero, or contains L, in which case the assumed k-bound applies.
This proves (1) for all closed ambient halfspaces.

There is an unavoidable limitation to this nonatomic transport. Taking
two opposite perpendicular caps gives k<=1/2. Every non-atomic measure
of mass k on a line has maximum halfspace depth exactly k/2. Thus using
only (1) and the line measure's center cannot give more than 1/4 for a
single continuous body. In particular this transport does not preserve
the required gamma_r, which exceeds 1/4. Atomic targets are not covered
by that limitation, but choosing a suitable atom would already require
the point-depth assertion one is trying to prove.

## 2. A maximally deep projected line need not contain a Grunbaum point

Let

    T={(x,y):x>=0,y>=0,x+y<=1}

with uniform probability measure, and put

    h=1-1/sqrt(2),  L={(x,y):y=h}.

The portion of T above L is a similar triangle of area fraction
(1-h)^2=1/2. Therefore every halfspace containing the entire line L has
measure at least 1/2=gamma_1. This is the best possible transversal
guarantee in one projected dimension.

Nevertheless no point of L has depth gamma_2=4/9. A point of L outside
T has depth zero. For a point (x,h) in T, its barycentric coordinates
relative to (0,0),(1,0),(0,1) are

    lambda_0=1-x-h, lambda_1=x, lambda_2=h.

The first two sum to 1/sqrt(2), so one is at least 1/(2sqrt(2)). If
lambda_i=s is such a coordinate, the closed vertex cap
{lambda_i>=s} contains the point and has area fraction (1-s)^2. Hence
every point of L has depth at most

    (1-1/(2sqrt(2)))^2=9/8-1/sqrt(2)<4/9.

For an exact verification of the strict inequality, it is equivalent
to 49/72<1/sqrt(2); squaring the positive quantities gives
2401/5184<2592/5184.

Thus even an optimal projected center-transversal does not automatically
lift to an exact-dimensional Grunbaum point on the chosen line. The
example uses one simplex and applies to two identical measures as well.
It rules out that proposed point-selection lemma, not the existence of
some other line through a suitable point.
